Discussion This study examined how cooperation and competition reconfigure a small-group epistemic system. Participants must learn, evaluate themselves, recognize others' expertise, and grant epistemic credit. The results reveal three dissociations. The first separates debate from factual learning. The second separates actual knowledge from the social recognition of knowledge. The third separates the level of epistemic credit from calibration accuracy. ### 5.1. Debate Can Be Cognitively Productive Without Additional Factual Learning After the individual search, recall, and evaluation sequence, factual scores did not increase substantially across the subsequent 20-minute debate followed by partner evaluation and argument recall/evaluation. The one-sided upper bound on the mean T3--T2 gain was only +0.052 points out of 20. All candidate gains from +0.10 points upward were rejected. This conclusion is more informative than a simple null test of T3--T2. It bounds the size of any positive gain across the full second sequence on the metric used; it does not isolate the debate itself. This result does not contradict possible benefits of argumentation. Discussion can improve error detection, the quality of reasons, decision making, or coordination without producing gains on a factual inventory. Wecker and Fischer (2014) specifically show that argumentative quality and domain-specific knowledge are distinct outcomes. Work by Mercier and colleagues also shows that cross-evaluation of arguments can improve reasoning (Mercier, 2016; Mercier et al., 2015). Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory helps explain this dissociation. A group can distribute part of the processing demand. But members must also communicate and coordinate (Kirschner et al., 2011, 2018). In MOVICI, participants must additionally evaluate human sources and locate their own epistemic position. The resources mobilized can therefore support several different cognitive outcomes. A future study could measure more directly what circulates during debate. For example, a small set of target facts could be linked to specific arguments and then tested after discussion. This approach would be lighter than exhaustive tracing of every piece of information while still allowing local learning to be identified. ### 5.2. Knowing, Recognizing Knowledge, and Granting Credit Are Distinct Properties The second contribution is the most important. The partner's objective expertise explains virtually none of the variance in attributed expertise. The estimated coefficient is close to zero. The slopes remain null in both conditions. In this task, the objective distribution of knowledge and the social distribution of recognized expertise are therefore largely decoupled. Evaluator expertise does not clearly correct this decoupling. Research on source evaluation might have suggested an expert advantage (Brand-Gruwel et al., 2017; Lucassen & Schraagen, 2011). The observed interaction points in that direction, but its interval is wide and includes zero. Error analyses also show no advantage. Knowing more therefore does not guarantee a better map of others' knowledge in this interaction. This result is not incompatible with the expertise literature. Evaluating the accuracy of content and inferring a person's overall competence are different tasks. MOVICI debate is relatively unscripted. Knowledge is distributed across several themes and speaking turns. Hinds (1999) also reminds us that expertise can distort representations of others' performance. This result requires a distinction between actual competence, recognized expertise, and epistemic credit. It does not show that power causes credit. It shows that competence possessed does not enjoy an automatic privilege in the social attribution of expertise. The distribution of knowledge is therefore not equivalent to the distribution of recognized expertise or epistemic credit. CAVL also distinguishes this episode-specific credit from more stabilized epistemic authority (Vayre et al., 2026b). The visibility analyses illustrate this openness to other cues. Under competition, word count and speech share are strongly associated with attributed expertise. Objective expertise is not. This contrast is consistent with work on confidence as a competence signal (Price & Stone, 2004) and dominance as a signal of influence (Anderson & Kilduff, 2009). It also connects with work on prestige. When direct competence is difficult to evaluate, deference and reputation can serve as useful shortcuts (Henrich & Gil-White, 2001; Jiménez & Mesoudi, 2019). Developmental research shows that this conversion of social cues into epistemic cues emerges early. Children use an informant's past reliability to decide whom to believe (Clément et al., 2004). They also infer competence differences from dominance cues (Charafeddine et al., 2015). Bernard et al. (2016) further showed a testimonial preference for a dominant agent. These results cannot be directly generalized to the adults in MOVICI. They nevertheless show that the link between perceived social position and epistemic credit can emerge early. The sociology of status allows us to go further. Competence expectations can structure who speaks, who is heard, and who influences others (Berger et al., 2002; Kalkhoff & Thye, 2006). Standards of recognition can also vary by status (Foschi, 2000). Bourdieu (1975) further distinguishes technical competence from socially recognized authority. MOVICI does not directly measure these mechanisms. It reveals the problem they can exploit: competence does not automatically make itself visible. This dissociation also has implications for transactive memory. A representation of 'who knows what' is useful only if it corresponds sufficiently well to the actual distribution of expertise (Hollingshead, 2000). Bringing competent people together is therefore not enough. The group must also be able to identify where competence lies and give it appropriate weight. ### 5.3. Relational Structure Reconfigures Credit and May Set the Stage for Epistemic Inequalities H2a should be interpreted cautiously. The primary under-crediting test was marginal (p = .057). Several closely related specifications nevertheless converge on greater under-crediting under competition. The signal therefore rests on a coherent set of analyses rather than on a single decisive test. For self-evaluation, the result is more robust. Competition does not simply increase mean confidence. It weakens the correspondence between confidence and actual knowledge. H3 reinforces this point. At T3, subjective expertise strongly tracks objective expertise under cooperation and barely does so under competition. Social comparison provides a plausible mechanism. Colpaert et al. (2015) show that cooperative versus competitive framing changes the effect of comparison on self-evaluation. Competence differences can serve as feedback under cooperation. They can also become a ranking concern under competition. Timing imposes a clear limit. The slope contrast is already suggestive at T2. The Expertise × Condition × Time interaction is not significant. We therefore cannot say that the debate itself created the difference. However, T3 error remains lower under cooperation after controlling for T2 error. This result is compatible with more precise adjustment across the full interactional sequence, which includes debate, partner evaluation, and argument recall/evaluation before T3. Behavioral results support the idea of relational reconfiguration. Competition increases attacks but not total speech quantity. It therefore changes the form of interaction more than its volume. This pattern is consistent with research on relational conflict regulation (Darnon et al., 2006, 2007; Sommet et al., 2014). Cooperation also strongly increases perceived benevolence. The condition → benevolence → under-crediting path is compatible with a role for this relational dimension. But it remains exploratory and noncausal. The link with epistemic injustice becomes relevant at this point. Fricker (2007) defines testimonial injustice as a credibility deficit arising from prejudice. Dotson (2011) also shows how practices of listening can produce silencing. Medina (2011, 2013) emphasizes the unequal distribution of epistemic authority and the importance of both credibility excesses and deficits. MOVICI measures neither oppression nor identity prejudice. The observed errors are therefore not, in themselves, injustices. MOVICI reveals a more basic condition. Social credit can be weakly coupled to objective competence. The resource-rational approach of Dosso et al. (2025) helps explain how this condition can become a mechanism. When direct evaluation is costly, credibility heuristics may carry more weight. If these cues are unequally distributed, an architecture already weakly sensitive to actual competence can transform social inequality into inequality of epistemic credit. Status theories then provide a bridge to social mechanisms of recognition. MOVICI's contribution is more specific. The study does not demonstrate a complete case of epistemic injustice. It identifies a possible sociocognitive microfoundation: knowing, recognizing knowledge, and granting credit are not spontaneously aligned. ## 6. Limitations and Future Directions First, the study includes 96 participants and 34 debates. Several dyadic or behavioral analyses use 29 to 30 debates. CR2 corrections reduce the risk of overly liberal inference, but they do not replace replication. H2a should be read primarily as a convergence of results. Second, H3 is supported at T3, but its timing remains open. The slope difference is already suggestive at T2. The interaction with time is not significant. Because T3 follows debate, partner evaluation, and argument recall/evaluation, the present design cannot isolate change caused by the debate alone. A replication could add measures immediately before and immediately after debate, before post-debate evaluation and recall, to separate these components. Third, objective and subjective scores are placed on a common metric. Rank analyses provide a useful robustness check. But any under-crediting index depends partly on this mapping. A future study could ask participants to estimate, on the same scale, both their own expected score and their partners' expected scores. Fourth, objective knowledge is measured with a factual inventory. This criterion is relevant to the task, but it does not exhaust expertise. A participant may be better at synthesis, argumentation, or recognizing the limits of their knowledge while having a similar factual score. The findings therefore concern factual expertise as measured here. Fifth, the proposed relational mechanisms remain associational. Visibility is not manipulated. Benevolence and credit are measured in the same phase. Targeted studies could isolate one mechanism at a time. For example, they could manipulate displayed confidence while holding actual expertise constant, or manipulate a status cue separately. Finally, the link with epistemic injustice remains proximal. A dedicated study could cross interdependence structure with a status or social-membership cue. It would need to be designed and powered for that test. This would allow researchers to examine whether competition amplifies systematic credibility deficits or excesses. ## 7. Conclusion In a small group, having knowledge is not enough. Members must also recognize where knowledge lies and calibrate their own position. In MOVICI, factual scores do not increase substantially across the debate followed by partner evaluation and argument recall/evaluation that comes after the individual search-recall-evaluation sequence. Interdependence structure is, however, related to epistemic credit toward others and self-calibration. Analyses converge on greater under-crediting under competition. They also show a stronger relation between objective and subjective expertise under cooperation. The broader result goes beyond this comparison. Partners' actual expertise barely predicts the expertise attributed to them. Having greater expertise oneself does not clearly improve this discrimination. The social distribution of epistemic credit can therefore acquire relative autonomy from the objective distribution of knowledge. This autonomy does not show that power replaces truth. It shows why cues of visibility, status, prestige, or dominance can shape recognition.
